title: Sandpit sprint reads + next steps (Nadia Romano)
content:
Context and purpose:
Quick personal capture from a 1-week sandpit sprint — triaging a handful of papers/blogs that look relevant to our KV-prefix/cache work and to batching heuristics. This is messy; meant to be consumable by Samir and Mira for the spike planning meeting on 2027-04-21.

Top-level takeaways (fast):
- Short papers that actually test in realistic inference loops (latency+throughput) are rare. Emphasize evals that report 99p latency and tail effects.
- KV-prefix caching + dynamic eviction looks promising for long-session apps; main tradeoff is extra memory pressure and more fragmented GPU kernels at evict time.
- Light quant-aware caching (store quantized keys) could save memory but must be validated for mismatch between cached states and runtime dequantization.

Papers / posts skimmed (notes):
1) "Adaptive KV-store for Long Contexts" (preprint, 2026) — TL;DR: eviction based on token age + token access frequency; uses compact fingerprints to detect repeated spans.
   - Why it matters: avoids full sequence recompute for repeated references across conversation turns.
   - Implementation concerns: compact fingerprint collisions cause stale cache hits; need a validation bit or checksum.
   - Quick experiment idea: instrument current KV cache codepath to keep per-key access counter (cheap) and simulate age-based eviction in a replay trace from product chat logs.

2) "Quantized KV: tradeoffs in low-bit caches" (blog + small code repo) — TL;DR: storing cached keys in 4-bit quantized form reduces memory ~2-3x but increases retrieval variance; authors propose per-block scale tables.
   - Key note: their latency numbers assume dequant happens on CPU and is free; on our stacks dequant on GPU matters.
   - Quick test: port their quant/dequant microbench to our kernel stack (cuda kernels we use in serving-runtime repo PR#812) and measure dequant latency at batch sizes 1, 2, 8.

3) "Prefix-aware batching for streaming chat" (ICLR workshop talk notes) — TL;DR: schedule short-latency prefixes ahead of long completions using two-level queues.
   - Relevance: could push down p99 for interactive flows while preserving throughput on bulk jobs.
   - Risk: complexity in scheduler + backpressure interactions with autoscaler.
   - Follow-up: prototype a scheduler shim in the local dev harness (simulate two queues and record p50/p90/p99).

Conference takeaways (in-person notes, messy):
- Conversations w/ other infra teams pointed to pragmatic heuristics: keep hot-key sets pinned for a sliding window instead of LRU full-set eviction. Works if hot set < 10% of total keys.
- Several teams adopted hybrid approach: GPU-resident compact cache + CPU-index for eviction decisions. Might be good fit for Dedicated customers with high SLOs.

Open questions (to decide in spike planning):
- What are the correct replay traces? Product chat logs are best but redaction + privacy steps required. Can CS provide a sanitized trace subset? (ask Mira).
- Memory budget target: for Dedicated customers in our SLO tier B, what's a reasonable KV-reserve per model? (bring to SRE/infra sync).
- How to measure correctness for quantized cache hits (false positive / negative rates)? Propose golden-run regression harness.

Concrete experiments (priority ordered):
1) Replay trace simulation: instrument access counts and run simulated age-based eviction offline. Measure hit rate, effective token reduction, and proxy tail latency using our local latency model.
   - Data needs: sample traces (10k sessions) — ask Mira for sanitized export.

2) Microbench: integrate the blog's 4-bit quantization microkernels into our serving-runtime testbed. Measure dequant cost on GPU (batch sizes 1,2,8) and end-to-end generation latency delta.
   - Owner: Samir (kernel port) + me (bench harness).

3) Scheduler shim: implement a two-queue scheduler in the dev harness and replay mixed workloads (interactive chat + bulk rerank jobs). Compare p99.
   - Risk: needs careful backpressure simulation so results are meaningful.

Notes-to-self / experiments logistics:
- Keep experiment PRs small and reviewable. Kernel work in a separate PR to avoid blocking dev harness changes.
- Tag any synthetic traces with a clear README for lineage.
- Add a lightweight eval that runs on nightly CI with a tiny trace; if regressions in p99 appear, alert spike channel.

Meeting agenda draft for 2027-04-21 (20-30m):
- 5m quick show-and-tell: one-slide summary of the quant microbench idea.
- 10m decide on trace access and what sanitized subset we can use.
- 10m assign owners + timeline (who does kernel port, who extracts traces, who wires up scheduler shim).

Action items (immediate):
- [ ] @Mira: can you confirm whether we can get a sanitized 10k-session chat trace by 2027-04-19? If yes, drop link in linked_artifacts.
- [ ] @Samir: prototype quant/dequant microbench on our GPU kernels (target: baseline numbers by 2027-04-22).
- [ ] @Nadia (me): write a short README for the replay trace format and a small generator for synthetic traces.

Random stray ideas (brain dump):
- Could a compact Bloom-fingerprint alongside each kv-key help reduce collision-check cost? Need to quantify extra mem vs saved validation work.
- Eviction schedule that favors spanning tokens (not just single key recency), i.e., evict contiguous ranges if they are cold. Might interact poorly with sparse attention patterns.

References / links (quick):
- "Adaptive KV-store for Long Contexts" (preprint) — saved copy in Confluence link above.
- Quantized KV blog + repo — link in slack thread #kv-cache-experiments.
- Serving-runtime PR for kernel infra that matters: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/812

If you read nothing else: focus on getting a decent replay trace and a microbench for dequant on GPU. Those two data points will tell us whether to invest more in quantized caches or to bias towards eviction heuristics.

End.
